_comment: Proposal 149 §14 — surface ownership contract. One row per admin surface, describing who may reach it (audience), which presentations exist (ops / admin / console), which layer owns the write path, whether a plan entitlement gates it, and what a limited surface is allowed to receive. Consumed by tests/Feature/SurfaceOwnershipTest.php, which fails when a console key in console-endpoints.json has no row, when a Filament surface file is absent from the contract, or when a row breaks the closed vocabularies. Add the row first, then the route. 'state' values: full (rendered, writes allowed), subset (rendered, reduced field set / reduced actions), read-only (rendered, no writes), inert (rendered and writable, but no runtime code reads the value - the form is not yet a behaviour), link-out (a link only), absent (not present on this surface), planned (not built). A surface in state subset, read-only or inert MUST declare a 'projection' — the server-side reduction it receives.

surfaces.title: Chat
surfaces.notes: Console-first. The admin links out rather than embedding a second chat implementation.

surfaces.title: Transcripts
surfaces.projection: Read-only list scoped to the current estate: session key, assistant, turn count, first user message (100 chars) and timestamps. Message bodies are read behind an explicit inspect modal. Deletion and retention are the store's prune() and the console's DELETE; the panel has no mutating action.
surfaces.notes: Shipped on `/admin` 2026-11-17 (§39) with `GET|POST|DELETE /api/v1/chat-transcripts` unchanged. Building it first required the same schema fix as §27 and §29: `nvoos_transcripts` had no tenant column and `session_id` was globally unique, so any console user could list and open every estate's conversations, and two estates that generated the same session key overwrote each other. The key is now `(tenant_id, session_id)`; `prune()` stays deliberately unscoped because retention is a server-owned job with no request estate.

surfaces.title: Agent memory
surfaces.projection: Read-only browser scoped to the current estate: title, agent, tier, importance, content preview, wing/room, expiry and timestamps, with the full content behind an inspect modal. Expired rows stay listed because recall filters them out — 'why did it forget' has to have an answer. No create/update/delete on the panel; the memory tools and the console API own writes.
surfaces.notes: Shipped on `/admin` 2026-11-17 (§40). Same schema-first story as §27, §29 and §39: `nvoos_memories` had no tenant column and `MemoryStore` named the table in all six methods, so `search()` spanned every estate and any console user could read, rewrite or delete another estate's memory by id. `listByAgent( agent_id )` was never a boundary — the agent id is a query parameter. The store now takes a tenant resolver and every method starts from one `query()` helper.

surfaces.title: Assistants
surfaces.notes: Both presentations write through the same assistant service; the Filament page adds no business rules.

surfaces.title: Assistant blueprints
surfaces.notes: Shipped on `/admin` 2026-11-17 (§53) as `/admin/blueprints`. Not read-only, and `writer` stays `shared`, because the write is genuinely one service: the page calls `BlueprintInstaller` — the same writer behind the console's install route — rather than the route itself, so there is no loopback HTTP hop and no second install path to keep in step. Building this slice found **nothing to fix**, which is the opposite result from §47 (toolkit records), §49 (shortcuts) and §51 (security snapshots): the installer already resolved the existing assistant with `where('tenant_id', …)` and set the tenant on create, and `BlueprintCatalogue::installedMap()` was already estate-scoped, so a title collision is an estate collision and another estate's assistant neither blocks an install here nor renders as installed. That is recorded explicitly so the next reader does not go looking for the defect the neighbouring slices all had. Overwrite is a separate confirmed control and updates the same assistant in place; each install and reinstall writes its own record-level audit row because `AuditAdminRequests` excludes `/livewire/update`. Access requires `manage_options` in addition to non-viewer membership, matching the `can:manage_options` group around the console route — a panel write reachable by a member the API refuses would be a promise the runtime breaks. The catalogue itself is code-shipped reference data mirrored from the Pro toolkits by `bin/sync-blueprints.php` and guarded by its `--check` mode, identical on every estate; only the installed flags are estate-scoped. WordPress hides blueprints whose toolkit is disabled in `wp_mcp_ai_settings`; this runtime lists every mirrored toolkit, because there is no equivalent settings surface and hiding a blueprint nobody could enable would be worse than showing it.

surfaces.title: Assistant export / import
surfaces.notes: Shipped on `/admin` 2026-11-17 (§54) as `/admin/portability`. `full`, not read-only, and `writer` stays `shared`, because both transports call one service: `App\Services\AssistantPortability`. The page calls it directly, the console's `POST /assistants/export|import` routes call it from a controller that now only parses and maps refusals. Building this slice found the worst tenancy defect of the run, in three independent paths: `export()` queried `Assistant` with no estate filter at all, so a `manage_options` user in one estate received **every** estate's assistants including system prompts and free-form `meta` (a bulk disclosure, not a scoping bug); `import()` resolved its slug-then-title conflict unscoped, so `mode=overwrite` could `fill()->save()` another estate's row; and `Assistant::create()` never set `tenant_id` (the model has no `creating` hook), so an import in estate B wrote into the column default, while the `is_default` reset ran `update()` across the whole table. Fixed by construction rather than by adding `where()` clauses one at a time: every read goes through an estate-scoped query and every write through `AssistantWriter`, which already owned estate assignment, per-estate slug uniqueness and per-estate default exclusivity — the controller's private `uniqueSlug()` copy is deleted, which also changes the duplicate suffix from `-copy` to `-2`, matching WordPress's `wp_insert_post()` behaviour. A bundle is a document, not authority: a `tenant_id` inside an entry is never read, so a pasted bundle cannot import into another estate. An `ids[]` entry that is unknown or belongs elsewhere is refused with 422 rather than silently dropped — an incomplete bundle is how a restore lands wrong — and the message says 'not in this estate' without distinguishing absent from foreign. On `/admin`: export renders the bundle in a textarea (visible, and nothing is stored server-side), import is preview-first with the write behind a confirm and disabled while 'Preview only' is ticked, each import writes a record-level audit row carrying counts and mode but never the bundle, and access requires `manage_options` in addition to non-viewer membership, matching the console's `can:manage_options` group. Export itself is not audited because it is a read; see §54's follow-ups.

surfaces.title: MCP Apps
surfaces.projection: Full on both presentations, and both replace the whole per-assistant list through McpAppsStore::replace(): the eight writable fields (label, server_url, connection_ref, auth_type, header_name, enabled, timeout, verify_ssl) are whitelisted server-side, the list is capped at 10, and `oauth_data` is never written. A token is accepted but sealed by CredentialStore, stored at `token_sealed`, and projected back only as a uniform mask — never a value, never a tail. A blank token AND a mask both mean `keep the stored one`, so a read → write round-trip cannot seal the mask as a credential. The token is carried across an update by `connection_ref`, or by `server_url` when the ref is blank: changing either is a different connection and does not carry it, which the panel states in the form. The panel's `assistantId` is a selector, re-resolved through `assistants.tenant_id` on every request — Assistant has no global tenant scope, so a tampered id resolves to null rather than another estate's assistant.
surfaces.notes: The eight writable fields are whitelisted server-side; token and oauth_data are never written. Shipped on `/admin` 2026-11-17 (§43) as a FULL surface — the list is the unit of edit on both presentations, so a per-record CRUD would be a third shape. Two things the panel adds over the console's editor: a write-only token field (the console's `toWritableApp()` strips it, so a connection created there could never be given one) and the mask guard in McpAppsStore — `McpAppsTest::test_a_read_projection_cannot_be_saved_back_as_a_token` pins that a bulk read → write keeps the sealed token instead of replacing it with `••••••••`. Estate scope is `assistants.tenant_id`, checked on selection and again on save.

surfaces.title: Teams and membership
surfaces.notes: TeamServiceInterface owns tenant assignment, slug and creator-as-owner. Carries the cross-tenant 404 test.

surfaces.title: Professions
surfaces.projection: No reduction: both presentations read App\Support\ProfessionCatalogue and return the same rows (slug, title, category, category_slug, description, expertise, tools_count). Neither presentation writes — the write path is save_profession, an AI tool rather than a form. The catalogue has two tiers since §170: a code-owned base and an estate overlay, merged with the overlay winning per slug, so every presentation shows an estate the same merged catalogue. The base is reference data rather than a tenant-owned record set, so BOPLA does not apply — and reducing it would break the console's profession selector, which exists to offer every profession including one an assistant does not have yet.
surfaces.notes: Shipped 2026-11-17 (§23). `writer` corrected from `admin` to `none` at the time: save_profession was not registered on this runtime, so no surface owned a write path. 2026-11-22 (§170): the writable overlay that note predicted has landed and `writer` moved from `none` to `shared` — shared because the AI tool writes while no panel does, not because two panels write. The overlay is `nvoos_professions`, tenant-scoped through the `Profession` model, merged by `OverlayProfessionRepository`. A save is copy-on-write: the row is seeded from the base record before the caller's fields are applied, so an update keeps the fields it was not given and the estate takes ownership of that row from the first edit. The panel stays read-only deliberately. Promotions `save_profession` to `ready` ends the objection that create/edit controls would lie about persistence, but it does not add those controls: the tool is the one writer, and a form would be the second.

surfaces.title: Tool catalogue
surfaces.projection: No reduction, and that is the decision rather than an omission. Both presentations read App\Support\ToolCatalogue and return the same rows (slug, name, description, required_capability, readiness, annotations); neither writes. Readiness is what separates a tool that works from one merely present in the package, so hiding it would make the catalogue useless for its one job.
surfaces.notes: Shipped 2026-11-17 (§22). The earlier note here proposed projecting the console down to 'the assistant's enabled tools plus presets'. That was wrong: ToolPicker reads this payload so an administrator can enable a tool the assistant does not have yet, and a catalogue is a reference list rather than a tenant-owned record set, so BOPLA does not apply to it.

surfaces.title: Per-tool daily quotas
surfaces.projection: No reduction and no console presentation: the page is the estate's own cost control, and the console has no key for it. Estate scoping comes from `ToolQuota`'s global scope (Proposal 153), so the page and the guard cannot disagree about whose limit is being read. The badge is computed against the busiest user, not the estate total, because the limit is enforced per caller; the estate total is shown as its own column because 'what is this tool costing us' is a different question. The create form's tool selector is read from the live registry, so a quota can only name a tool that can run.
surfaces.notes: Shipped 2026-11-23 (§176), the `token_manager` -> `per_tool` view. This row was previously MISSING from the contract entirely, along with the orchestration `tools` view: §167.3 warned that the inventory was never re-derived from the WordPress menu, so a `?tab=`/`?view=` sub-page could be invisible here, and these were the first two instances found. Enforcement is a `tools/pre_execute` waterfall listener (not a monotonic guard) so a refusal surfaces as `tool_denied` carrying the quota's own message, which the model can read and route around; recording is an `AfterToolExecution` listener, so a refused call is never counted — otherwise a model could exhaust a quota by retrying. Cost is estimated from the size of the tool result (`strlen / 4`), the same ratio as WordPress's `estimate_tokens()`, because a tool body makes no provider call and therefore has no invoice line to attribute. A tool with no row, a disabled row and a zero limit are all unmetered: a control nobody configured must not refuse anybody. Multipliers are deliberately NOT ported — WordPress multiplies a per-user tier base, and this runtime has no claim tiers, so a multiplier field would render and change nothing (`inert`, which this contract refuses to count as parity). `ToolQuotaStore::prune()` bounds the usage table; the master switch is `oos.tool_quotas.enabled`, which also stops the per-call upsert.

surfaces.title: Tool orchestration settings (per-tool flags and force-sync)
surfaces.notes: Recorded 2026-11-23 (§176). The WordPress `orchestration` -> `tools` view writes per-tool capability-flag overrides (`wp_mcp_ai_tool_capability_flags`) and a force-synchronous set (`wp_mcp_ai_tool_force_sync`). It was invisible here because §167's inventory was never re-derived from the WordPress menu. NOT the same surface as `tools`: that row is the read-only catalogue and stays `writer: none`. The prerequisite is a seam, not a page — guards read flags through `ToolResolverInterface`, so the override belongs in a resolver decorator, and it must be NARROW-ONLY (a flag may be added to the gated set, never removed): an estate-level control that could clear `read-only` or `destructive` would be an authority grant dressed as a setting. MCP's own position is that annotations are untrusted hints and the contract lives in the runtime, which is what makes widen-only-overrides indefensible.

surfaces.title: Orchestration thresholds and per-call token caps
surfaces.notes: Recorded 2026-11-23 (§176). The WordPress `orchestration` -> `thresholds` view is 24 fields: memory and error-rate warn/critical bands, budget priorities, health reductions, low/medium/high tier max tokens, `per_call_token_limit` and `per_session_token_limit` with their two toggles, compression, and predictive confidence. The budget half already has a home (`budgets`, USD over a window) and the per-tool half shipped in `tool-quotas`; what has no reader is the warn/critical banding and the per-call/per-session caps, which are loop bounds rather than configuration. They need a `lib/core` contract (the orchestrator's `tokenBudget` is a single deployment value today, not a per-call ceiling) before a page can mean anything.

surfaces.title: Orchestration presets
surfaces.notes: Recorded 2026-11-23 (§176). WordPress ships named bundles that write the `settings` and `thresholds` groups at once, with a recommendation engine (`WP_MCP_AI_Tool_Recommendations`) that reports which tools differ from the chosen preset. A preset over fields that do not exist yet would be a button that writes nothing, so this surface is ordered after `orchestration.thresholds` and `orchestration.tool-overrides` — the same dependency the WordPress page has, where the preset is a projection over those two groups.

surfaces.title: Orchestration settings
surfaces.notes: Recorded 2026-11-23 (§176). 35 toggles on the WordPress page. Most are NOT portable as-is because the software they configure does not exist on this runtime — RabbitMQ, DSPy/`use_ts_build`, SSE duration, cron orchestration, capacity-aware routing. The subset that does have meaning (budget management, semantic compression, memory retention) is already enforced by lib/core config rather than by a stored setting, so a page over it would be a second truth. Recorded as `planned` rather than built: the honest move is to map each toggle to a reader first, and hide the ones with no reader the way §104 hides the ten authentication keys.

surfaces.title: Memory health
surfaces.notes: Recorded 2026-11-23 (§176). The WordPress view reports memory-specific health signals and links back to the thresholds that drive its warn/critical bands. It is NOT `/admin/memory`: that page browses what an assistant has stored, while this is a read-only health summary over the same store (count, growth, dormancy against `memory_dormancy_days`). Ordering follows `orchestration.thresholds`, because the bands it renders are the fields that surface writes.

surfaces.title: DSPy efficiency
surfaces.notes: Recorded 2026-11-23 (§176). WordPress reads DSPy compile artifacts (`use_ts_build`, speculative block size and acceptance threshold) from a Python build pipeline this runtime does not run. `nvoos_routing_metrics` and the harness trace store could support an efficiency page, but it would be a NEW surface rather than a port — the WordPress page describes configuration for software that is absent here, the same judgement §104 applies to the ten authentication keys.

surfaces.title: RabbitMQ
surfaces.notes: Recorded 2026-11-23 (§176) as declined, not missing. This runtime queues with the database/Redis driver (`nvoos_jobs`, `/ops/queue`), so the WordPress page's broker connection, queue depths and consumer controls describe infrastructure that does not exist here. `/ops/queue` is the surface with the same job, and the contract records the absence rather than leaving a reader to wonder whether it was overlooked.

surfaces.title: Token usage per site
surfaces.notes: Recorded 2026-11-23 (§176) as declined, not missing. The WordPress view is a multisite report: usage rolled up per site in a network. This runtime's unit is the estate (`nvoos_token_usage.tenant_id`), and an estate is not a site — a deployment serves many estates, not many sites under one. The estate breakdown already exists on `/ops/token-usage` and `/ops/token-analytics`, so a 'per site' page here would be the same rows under a misleading label.

surfaces.title: Estate settings
surfaces.projection: Read: the estate catalogue — every field the estate owns, with operator-scope fields included but masked as managed. Write: writableFor('admin'), which excludes operator scope, so a crafted payload naming enable_logging or ollama_endpoint is ignored rather than rejected. Sensitive fields are masked on read and blank means unchanged.
surfaces.notes: Console projection shipped 2026-11-17 (§15). Ownership shipped 2026-11-17 (§16): tenant/user scope lives in nvoos_tenant_settings keyed by (tenant_id, key). The page shipped 2026-11-17 (§17): generated from SettingsSchema, so a new field is one edit. Operator-scope fields render disabled under the S-1 hint rather than being omitted.

surfaces.title: Platform settings
surfaces.projection: Admin renders the operator-scope fields disabled with the S-1 hint (subset: same values, no write). Ops renders writableFor('ops') — operator scope only — and writes the platform layer, so one save applies to every estate. Estate fields are deliberately absent from /ops: that panel has no estate selected, so editing one would silently change the default estate.
surfaces.notes: Carries enable_logging and ollama_endpoint. ollama_endpoint became operator scope with S-5: it is a URL the server fetches, so a tenant form choosing it is an SSRF primitive. Customers still select the ollama provider and model on the estate surface.

surfaces.title: Approvals
surfaces.projection: Read-only queue scoped to the current estate: id, status, tool, requester, reason, queued/expiry and timestamps, with the queued arguments and the resolution behind an inspect modal. No approve/deny on the panel — resolving stays the console's write, and a panel action would need its own audit row first (§25).
surfaces.notes: Shipped on `/admin` 2026-11-17 (§41). Schema-first like §27/§29/§39/§40: `nvoos_approvals` had no tenant column and `ApprovalsController` named the table in `index`, `store` and `resolve`, so any estate administrator could list the whole queue and **approve or deny another estate's gated tool call**. `resolve` is the sharp edge, as `fire` was in §29. Approve/deny on the panel is the recorded next step: it flips `writer` to `shared` and must write a record-level audit row, because panel traffic goes over `/livewire/update`, which the request audit skips.

surfaces.title: Schedules, triggers and presets
surfaces.projection: No field reduction — the reduction is actions: the panel lists workflows and triggers and offers no create/edit/delete/fire, because the console owns this CRUD by ruling (§13.1) and a second writer would maintain one page twice. Two omissions are deliberate and cheap: a trigger's `webhook_url` is reduced to its HOST plus a has_webhook flag, because webhook providers put the secret in the path; and `config` is reduced to its `schedule` value rather than echoed whole. Both sets are estate-scoped through TenantContext, which SetTenantContext pins to the panel tenant on every /admin request.
surfaces.notes: Console-owned by ruling (149 §13.1). Definitions are CRUD; rebuilding them in Filament would maintain one page twice. Shipped as a read-only view 2026-11-17 (§30), unblocked by §29: `nvoos_triggers` gained `tenant_id` and TriggersController now scopes every query, so the list is honest. Before that the console's `triggers` key was cross-estate, and a panel over it would have leaked every estate's triggers twice. The page shows workflows + triggers only: `scheduleManager` is already served by `/ops/scheduler` and `workflowPresets` has no reader.

surfaces.title: Workflow runs and orchestration stats
surfaces.projection: Run rows plus node outcomes; no graph mutation, no re-run from this surface. Reads go through App\Support\WorkflowRuns in both presentations, and WorkflowRun applies a tenant global scope, so /admin and the console cannot disagree about which runs exist or what a summary contains.
surfaces.notes: Shipped 2026-11-17 (§18). Run records acquired tenant_id in the same slice, because a read-only list over an unscoped table would expose another estate's per-node payload. Definitions stay console-owned (§13.1); only the after-the-fact log is ported.

surfaces.title: Workflow builder
surfaces.notes: React canvas bundled into the admin in Wave 6; never rebuilt in Livewire.

surfaces.title: Security audit, monitor and training
surfaces.projection: A chart-free projection over saved settings snapshots, operator-wide because `/ops` has no estate selected: per-estate counts, then the newest rows with estate, label, recorded-at and key count, and a detail panel whose settings are masked at render as well as at write time. Explicitly absent: the posture scan, the header preview, the self-test and the posture chart — the first three are console checks run on demand and the chart is Wave 6 (canvas bundle, §7.10). Nothing on either presentation writes.
surfaces.notes: The `/admin` half shipped 2026-11-17 (§51) as `/admin/security`; the `/ops` half shipped 2026-11-22 (§171), and the live security-monitor chart remains Wave 6 (canvas bundle, §7.10). Building the admin half exposed a tenancy defect: `nvoos_security_snapshots` had no estate column while its payload is the estate's settings, so `GET /security/snapshots` listed every estate and `POST /security/restore` would copy another estate's configuration into the caller's settings — a cross-estate configuration disclosure and write. The table now carries `tenant_id` and every estate-scoped statement goes through `App\Support\Security\SecuritySnapshotStore`. `writer` moved from `shared` to `console` because neither panel has a write: creating and restoring snapshots remain console actions (§16's one-writer rule). The four WordPress pages behind this row (audit dashboard, monitor, training, supplier security) are not ported one-to-one: the audit log already lives at `/ops/audit-log`, the monitor chart is Wave 6, and training/supplier records have no store on this runtime. The snapshot row's button was dead until §53: `@js()` does not compile inside a `<x-filament::…>` attribute, so the attribute shipped verbatim and Livewire threw in the browser while every PHP test passed; it now uses a `{{ Js::from(...) }}` echo, and `AdminPanelBladeTest` bans the directive in panel views. §171 added a second READER rather than loosening the store's scope: `App\Support\Security\SecuritySnapshotOverview` is unfiltered because its audience is the operator panel, and `SecuritySnapshotStore` stays estate-filtered because its payload is one estate's configuration. Both presentations mask through one helper (`SecuritySnapshotStore::maskedRows()`), so they cannot drift on which keys are sensitive.

surfaces.title: Operations, diagnostics and cost
surfaces.projection: Aggregates only. A probe returns a rendered result summary — status, one actionable sentence and label/value rows — never a raw provider payload. Credentials appear as "configured"/"no credentials"; there is no mask, no key and no URL with a query string, because the probe result type has no field for one.
surfaces.notes: Shipped on `/ops` 2026-11-17 (§48) as `/ops/diagnostics`, closing the last WordPress screens this runtime did not have: Tools → Provider Test, MCP Server Diagnostic and REST Context Diagnostic, plus the free half of Test Assistant. Six probe surfaces were proposed (§7.8) with one renderer; four shipped — `provider`, `rest`, `mcp`, `assistant`. `test model`, `test profession` and `test team` are deliberately NOT built: the WordPress pages are chat UIs with a selector, and a panel copy would be a second chat surface whose only difference is which config it hydrates. The console owns chat, so those three stay unbuilt rather than faked. `writer` moved from `ops` to `none` for §31's reason: every probe re-runs on demand and nothing is persisted, so there is no write path to own. §82 added `/ops/token-usage` beside it: per-user aggregates over the same cost table, read-only, with no new console key and no new write path.

surfaces.title: Measurement dashboard
surfaces.projection: The catalogue is the WordPress vocabulary, verbatim: 21 definitions across the chat, tool, stream and eval packs, each with unit, direction, counter-metric and privacy tier. Every row is rendered — including the ten this runtime cannot produce — because a catalogue that hid its gaps would be the empty-list page §85.2 warned about. Values are cross-estate: this is the operator surface. No export, no write.
surfaces.notes: Recorded 2026-11-17 (149 §45) after the admin-inventory audit (§44) found it outside both counted trees: `includes/admin/measurement/` attaches a Measurement page to the settings dashboard (`wp-mcp-ai-dashboard`) and falls back to Tools when that menu is absent. It is a NEW surface, not a port of a probe: the WordPress page lists registered metrics (privacy tier, counter-metric pairing), verifiers (independence profile), reward functions (anti-gaming text), eval suites (case counts) and the most recent collector-buffer events; its admin-post handler clears the buffer, downloads a JSON export and resets a persistent budget envelope — so it has a writer, unlike a pure probe. That is product data, which is why it is not folded into `platform-operations` (runtime probes and cost aggregates). Planned rather than `absent` because metrics and evals are product features rather than WordPress idioms; the prerequisite is the data model (metric and eval-run stores), not a renderer — the WordPress page is itself pre-PR-4 read-only. The third store this row used to claim, budgets, became its own surface in §92/§93: it needed no producer, only a limit over rows already written. Decision recorded 2026-11-19 (149 §96, Proposal 155): the surface will be a DERIVED catalogue, not three stores. Metric definitions are code rather than rows (no `nvoos_metrics`), values are queries over `nvoos_token_usage`, `nvoos_harness_trace_records` and `nvoos_routing_metrics`, and the page names the thirteen of twenty-one metrics this runtime cannot produce instead of rendering zeros. Verifiers, rewards and eval suites stay planned by decision (D5): they judge an answer, not a request, and no harness exists on either runtime. Row remains `planned` until slice M1 (`/ops/metrics`). 2026-11-19 (§99): shipped as a DERIVED catalogue. Metric definitions are code (`App\Support\Metrics\MetricCatalogue`), not rows, and values are queries over `nvoos_token_usage` and `nvoos_harness_trace_records` — no `nvoos_metrics` table. Ten of the 21 are produced (six token/chat, four tool from the §98 `tool` trace record), one is partial (`chat.turn.error.count`), ten are not produced and say why. A metric with no producer renders its reason, never a zero; and when the window holds no trace records the trace-derived rows are blank rather than zero, because capture is per assistant and opt-in. Verifiers, rewards and eval suites remain `planned` by decision (155 D5).

surfaces.title: Spend and limits
surfaces.projection: The estate-facing page renders only the current estate's budgets (the model's tenant scope), with spend, limit, used percentage and enabled state. No mutating action: a limit the limited party can raise is a self-throttle, not a control (154 D8).
surfaces.notes: Split out of `measurement` in §92/§93 (Proposal 154). A budget is a limit over records that already exist: `nvoos_token_usage` is written by the §81/§86 pipeline and carries `cost` and an estate, so the store holds only `(tenant_id, window, limit_usd, warn_at, enabled)` and consumption is `SUM(cost)` over the window. Spend is deliberately not stored, so a budget and the cost pages cannot disagree. Enforcement is pre-flight at the chat entry points and `AgentNodeRunner`: 429 `budget_exceeded`, 503 `budget_unverifiable` (fail closed), and a zero limit reads as 'no limit'. §92 shipped the enforcement, §93 the two surfaces.

surfaces.title: Estate assistant credentials
surfaces.projection: Credentials for the estate's OWN assistants only: the estate's assistant ids resolve first, and the token list is filtered by the literal `oos-assistant-{id}` names those ids produce. Metadata only — the token hash is never selected. revoke/delete answer 404 for an assistant outside the estate. lift is 404 by design: this runtime keeps no persisted restrictions. On `/admin` the reduction is actions, not fields: list and revoke are offered, issuing is not, because issuing is rotation and rotation is the operator surface (`credentials.assistant`, writer: ops), which creates the replacement before deleting the old ids.
surfaces.notes: Shipped as the console's token-manager; estate-scoped 2026-11-17 (§19). Before that the listing and the revoke path used the whole `oos-assistant-*` range, so one estate could read and revoke another estate's credentials — a cross-tenant write. Distinct from operator rotation (/ops/credentials), which is deliberately cross-estate. The contract previously mislabelled this key as personal access tokens; §19 corrected it. §24 adds the `/admin` presentation and extracts App\Support\EstateCredentials so the console and the panel share one reader and one revoke primitive — a second revoke path would drift on the one rule that matters (never across estates). The page scopes by the panel tenant, not by TenantContext, because Filament tenancy does not populate that context on every request.

surfaces.title: Personal access tokens
surfaces.projection: Ownership, not capability: every read and the revoke path filter on the authenticated user's id, and a token id belonging to someone else answers 404 rather than disclosing that it exists. Metadata only — the hash column is never selected, so the plaintext exists solely in the response to the mint call and nowhere else. The routes sit OUTSIDE ResolveApiTenant because a token is not estate data: it belongs to a person across every estate they can reach. Abilities are not the authority — nothing in this runtime calls tokenCan() or applies abilities: middleware, so authorization comes from the user's current role through CapabilityMap, and the stored ability is ['*'] because that is the truth. No ability selector and no "never expires" option are offered: one would be an unenforced promise, the other a permanent credential. On `/ops` (§114) the same surface is read cross-estate and READ-ONLY: the inventory selects metadata only (the hash column is still never selected, and a test asserts the select list rather than the rendered rows), and it presents the holder's memberships as REACH, not as the token's scope — a token has no estate, so presenting memberships as scope would describe a narrowing nothing enforces. The read writes one audit row per visit, with the estate that was narrowed to as the record id, because a cross-tenant administrative read must be explicit, separately authorized and auditable.
surfaces.notes: Shipped on `/admin` 2026-11-17 (§26) with GET/POST/DELETE `/api/v1/personal-tokens`. `writer` narrowed from `shared` to `admin`: the operator cross-estate view is still unbuilt, and pretending otherwise would mark a write path that does not exist. Personal tokens are named `oos-personal:*` so `credentials.estate` and the console token manager (`oos-assistant-*` exact names) can never list them, and this surface cannot list assistant credentials. The earlier label on this row (`tokenManager`) was wrong and §19 corrected it. §114 added the read-only cross-estate inventory on `/ops` (`TokenInventory`), which closed the last `planned` row on that panel; `writer` deliberately stays `admin`, because a cross-estate REVOKE is a separate decision that has not been taken. `audience` widened from `tenant-admin` to `operator`, following the convention `budgets` and `settings.platform` already use when `ops` reaches `full`.

surfaces.title: Remote sites
surfaces.projection: Estate-scoped since §27: every read and write goes through RemoteSiteStore::query(), which filters on `tenant_id` read from a resolver at query time. A connection id from another estate answers 404 on update, delete and test — the test route matters most, because it sends the row's sealed credentials to the URL the row names. Secrets are masked uniformly; credentialsFor() is the only opener and is runtime-only. On `/admin` the reduction is ACTIONS, not fields: list, test, enable/disable and delete are offered; create and edit are not, because the console's wizard owns authoring (it renders each type's field schema from RemoteSiteTypes and splits the flat payload server-side), and a second authoring form would be that wizard twice with a second place to keep the secret/non-secret split correct. The panel renders presence, never a credential — `has_credentials` only, not the mask — and shows the endpoint as host + path: query and fragment are dropped because a provider can put a secret there (§30's webhook_url rule). Access requires `manage_options` in addition to panel membership, matching the REST surface.
surfaces.notes: Credentials are masked uniformly; credentialsFor() is the only opener and is runtime-only. §27 added `tenant_id` to `nvoos_remote_sites`: before it the table had no tenant column and the store read and wrote it unscoped while the routes already resolved an estate, so any estate administrator could list, edit, delete and TEST every other estate's connections — a cross-tenant write, the same defect class as §19. Existing rows default to `default` because no signal can attribute them to another estate. The `/admin` page shipped 2026-11-17 (§42) as a SUBSET: the store is the boundary (a foreign id is `null`, so a tampered armed state deletes nothing), the shared RemoteSiteVerifier is the Test action so the panel and the console cannot report differently about one endpoint, and test/enable/disable/delete each write their own audit row because Livewire traffic is excluded from the request-level audit.

surfaces.title: Skills, shortcuts and slash commands
surfaces.projection: Three read-only lists. Skills: name, description, licence and compatibility from the configured skills directory, plus that directory so an empty list is explainable. Shortcuts: the normalised label/payload/tool/description/category/icon for one assistant resolved inside the current estate. Slash commands: name, description, usage, parameters and category for the commands the signed-in account may run, filtered by the executor's own capability check. No install, execute, clear or delete control; all four are writes and the console owns them.
surfaces.notes: Shipped on `/admin` 2026-11-17 (§49). The WordPress manager (install from raw SKILL.md or a remote catalogue, replace, delete) stays absent, and the WP slash-command dashboard's execute/execute-workflow/clear-history actions are not ported: `writer` is `console`, and a panel control would create a second command path. Execution history is also not rendered — `nvoos_slash_command_audit` has no `tenant_id`, so a tenant-scoped page could only show it by leaking across estates or inventing a users-join; that is a §47-class schema gap, recorded rather than papered over. Building the slice exposed the same class of defect in `ToolShortcutsController`: it resolved the assistant with a bare `find()` and the default with a bare `is_default` lookup, so an id from another estate returned that estate's shortcut configuration and a foreign default could win the fallback. Both now resolve through `App\Services\AssistantShortcutCatalogue`, which the page also uses.

surfaces.title: OKF knowledge bundles
surfaces.projection: Read-only bundle and concept views over the deployment's knowledge directory. Bundles: name, concept/stale/deprecated counts, types, trust-tier distribution, broken-internal-link count. Concepts: id, title, type, status, trust tier, staleness and tags for one bundle, filtered server-side and capped with the pre-cap total printed. Concept detail: only the shared frontmatter allowlist plus body and resolved internal links. No bundle create, replace, delete or write control.
surfaces.notes: Shipped on `/admin` 2026-11-17 (§50). The row named `okf-bundle-manager-admin-page` — bundle CRUD — but only the read half is portable: `WP_MCP_AI_OKF_Writer` lives in the plugin and this runtime has no OKF writer, so `writer` moved from `console` to `none` and the console state from `full` to `read-only` (its five routes are all GETs). Knowledge is deployment-global, not estate data: one directory at `config('oos.okf.path')` serves every estate, which the page states rather than implying the list is the tenant's own. `/okf/skills` stays honest-empty because there is no grant store; the page renders no grant section that could only be empty. Building it moved the frontmatter allowlist to `OkfCatalogue::FRONTMATTER_ALLOWLIST` + `allowlisted()` so the controller and the page cannot drift. The bundle and concept row buttons were dead until §53: `@js()` does not compile inside a `<x-filament::…>` attribute (the component tag compiler makes the value a string literal) and breaks a single-quoted attribute on a plain element, so Livewire threw `Missing closing parenthesis` in the browser while every PHP test passed. Both now use `{{ Js::from(...) }}` echoes and `AdminPanelBladeTest` bans the directive in panel views.

surfaces.title: Paper Store and record schemas
surfaces.projection: Read-only browse over the deployment's Paper Store: collection names with record counts, one collection's records filtered by status and tag (capped, with the pre-cap total printed), a cross-collection search over title and description, and one record's description, body, tags and meta. Plus the record-schema catalogue `GET /pro/records/schema` serves. No create, edit or delete control.
surfaces.notes: Shipped on `/admin` 2026-11-17 (§52). **Deliberately NOT estate-scoped, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** Unlike §47 (toolkit records), §49 (shortcuts) and §51 (security snapshots), the Paper Store holds curated shared knowledge — research records, prompts, workflows, brand kits — and has no owner column on either runtime; the contract's promise is that 'a record written by WordPress is readable here and vice versa'. Adding `tenant_id` would break that cross-runtime property and split a shared library. The page states the sharing instead of implying the list is the tenant's own. The panel is read-only because the console owns CRUD and the row is slated for the Wave 3 manifest engine, which will render records from a schema rather than from a second hand-written form; `writer` moved from `shared` to `console` to match. Building it moved the four-entity records catalogue from `RecordsController` to `App\Support\RecordsSchema` so the API and the page cannot advertise different entities. The page's search loop deliberately mirrors the controller rather than extracting a service: that glue is what the manifest engine replaces. Every row button on this page was dead until §53 — both the `<x-filament::…>` attributes (`@js()` never compiles there) and the plain `<button>` in search results (single-quoted attribute colliding with `Js::from()`'s single quotes). They now use `{{ Js::from(...) }}` echoes in double-quoted attributes; `AdminPanelBladeTest` fails the build on either variant.

surfaces.title: Dashboard schemas
surfaces.projection: Read-only, on one estate. Read: the dashboards this runtime can actually feed (today `eca` only), rendered from the same DashboardGatherer the console's REST endpoint calls, so a figure cannot read differently on the two surfaces. Filters are whitelisted against the catalogue and applied live. A dashboard whose store does NOT exist here is ABSENT from the page, not disabled: a greyed control promises an enabled state the reader can reach, and `connectors` and `members` have no store to switch on (the same line §104 drew for inapplicable settings and S-3 for unlicensed toolkits). A dashboard whose store exists but whose toolkit is off (`enable_eca_management`, default off) IS shown, naming the toggle, because that reader can fix it in two clicks. A metric that was not computed renders an em dash, never 0. Distributions render as labelled bars carrying their value as text, including the chart the catalogue calls a `donut`: the panel has no chart library, and bars are more precise for ranking than pie or donut (Hill, Information Visualization 2025).
surfaces.notes: Redundancy review 2026-11-17 (149-dashboards-redundancy-review.md): 10 dashboards, two genuine duplicates. ezuite and flowhub share an identical render spec (five metrics, one name/count list) and differ only in data source; health and vitals share filters and structure and differ only in columns, gated by two different toolkit flags. Recommendation: 10 -> 7 (Connector health = ezuite + flowhub + shopify; Member metrics = health + vitals; cre, law, registration, eca and observability unchanged). Not implemented: WordPress is the catalogue's source of truth, DashboardsTest pins the disabled set, and retired ids need aliases in console URLs and WP widget registration. Wave 5 with a matching WP change. Decided 2026-11-20 (158 D1): the 10 -> 7 merge is accepted as written, with aliases for the retired ids and a WordPress-first change in the same pass. The row stays `planned` until that lands; what is decided is the shape of the future row, not the row. **Built 2026-11-20 (plan §112):** both catalogues now declare seven surfaces. A merged dashboard declares `sections` in the catalogue and `get_schema()` expands the visible ones into the flat render contract, namespacing each key by its section (`ezuite_in_stock`, `vitals_history`) because two connectors both publish `in_stock`; `group` carries the section label, additively. Gating is unchanged in effect: each section keeps its old flag, the whole surface is available when any section is, and the Medical Vitals BC fallback (dedicated toggle wins when saved, otherwise follows Health & Wellness) survives in both the section rule and the candidate-flag list. The five retired ids resolve through `aliases()`, published in the schema envelope; the data endpoint reports the RESOLVED id, and resolving is not a grant — the replacement's own gate still applies. A connector answering 501 degrades to `<section>_error` with the other sections intact; any other error propagates, and the member surface still 400s on a missing member. The console needed no runtime change (the picker is catalogue-driven); its types gained the optional fields. Known gap: the disabled-state hint names one raw flag of up to three, because fixing it properly needs a flag-to-label map (plan §112.6). The row remains `planned` — what shipped is the catalogue on both runtimes, not a Laravel page.

surfaces.title: Toolkit domain surfaces
surfaces.projection: Settings, the entity workbench (list + server-side search + armed delete), the dashboard cards, the research wizard and the consolidate scan all render from the manifest through ToolkitEngine. The free-form record editor stays in the console workbench; the ONE write the panel performs beyond deletion is the research draft save, which goes through createRecord so the manifest's column validation remains the single gate into the table. research/consolidate shipped on the panel in Wave 4 (2026-11-18) and are entity-scoped: a manifest with no entities answers 404 on both rather than render an empty wizard.
surfaces.notes: Wave 3 renderer shipped 2026-11-18 (plan §56). One index page lists the manifests the estate's entitlement allows; one parameterised page renders `/admin/{estate}/toolkits/{toolkit}/{screen}` from data — a new toolkit is a manifest commit, not a page. Settings tabs come from `tab_labels`/`tab` (single General tab when absent). An unlicensed toolkit is absent from the catalogue and answers 404 to a direct URL, indistinguishable from an unknown one (R4). Entity delete is armed two-step and audited with keys only — a diff never carries a secret value.

surfaces.title: Command centre
surfaces.projection: Read: one estate's overview - six KPIs, the agent status map and the last 8 feed entries, assembled by App\Support\CommandCentre\CommandCentreReport and shared with GET /api/v1/pro/command-center/overview. No write path on either surface: approvals and their decisions are the `approvals` row. Five of the WordPress surface's seven tabs are separate rows here (approvals, automation-runs, token-analytics, site-health, diagnostics) and are deliberately not duplicated; `strategy` has no producer in this runtime.

surfaces.title: Media
surfaces.projection: Read: one estate's library - totals, alt and next-gen coverage, and a paginated file list - from App\Support\Media\MediaLibrary, the same projection GET /api/v1/pro/media-cc/health serves. Scoped by nvoos_files.tenant_id, on the page and on the API. Writes (upload, alt text) stay on the console; the panel has no action, so it carries no Livewire-audit obligation. Queue counts and derivative savings are deliberately not shown: nvoos_jobs carries no estate, and savings already appear beside the worker health the console renders.
surfaces.notes: mediaCc is connected-service: the key reports false when no Media Worker is configured. Proposal 149 §109: nvoos_files gained a tenant_id in the §18 shape, so the page, the API and the compression sweep are scoped, and a foreign file id answers 404 rather than 403. Rows written before that migration read as `default` and cannot recover their estate. MediaSweeper::inFlight() stays platform-wide because nvoos_jobs carries no estate - the queue is one worker pool, the same reading §106 records for the command centre's active_tasks.

surfaces.title: Chat channels
surfaces.projection: Settings only. The four settings the WordPress screen actually persists — enable_logging, enable_rate_limiting, verify_webhook_signatures and optimization_message_retention_days — render from chat-channels.json through ToolkitEngine at /admin/{estate}/toolkits/chat-channels/settings. The per-platform credential panels are absent by evidence, not by omission: they are not in the option's sanitize_settings() whitelist, so the WordPress screen discards them on save, and channel credentials belong to Connections. No entity workbench and no dashboard cards, because the family owns no nvoos_toolkit_records rows.
surfaces.notes: toolkit-shaped: the manifest (chat-channels.json) is the entitlement hook and renders the settings screen. The row moved planned -> subset when that manifest shipped (PR #7906): a settings-only reduction is a rendered surface with a projection, not an absence.

surfaces.title: WordPress bridge base
surfaces.notes: WordPress-only. No admin equivalent by design (149 Appendix B: N).

surfaces.title: Connected products
surfaces.notes: external-product: discovered through a host probe, never ported. No admin page is planned.

surfaces.title: Estates and licences
surfaces.notes: Licence key is write-only; is_operator and slug are not editable; TenantPolicy denies create and delete.

surfaces.title: Models and rates
surfaces.notes: Text/chat models from resources/model-catalog.json (251 models, 18 providers): context, TPM/RPM, per-1M input/output prices, fallback and lifecycle. Operator scope because rates and limits are provider reference data; an estate selects a model, it does not rewrite the price. Sync inserts missing models and never overwrites an edited row. Media models are a separate capability catalogue (media-model-catalog.json) with per-image/per-second prices and are not part of this surface.

surfaces.title: Failed jobs (DLQ)
surfaces.notes: Laravel failed_jobs, distinct from the console's nvoos_jobs DLQ: different producers, different questions. The WordPress Job Queue page (`class-wp-mcp-ai-async-job-queue.php`, a submenu under `wp-mcp-ai`) lists *pending* async jobs; this surface covers failed jobs only (retry/forget/flush), and `/diagnostics/overview` reports the counts. A pending-job listing is not exposed — recorded by the admin-inventory audit (149 §44) rather than left implicit.

surfaces.title: Scheduler liveness
surfaces.notes: Liveness only. Definitions belong to the console; clocks stay owned by ScheduleRunner.

surfaces.title: Assistant credentials
surfaces.notes: Rotation issues the replacement before deleting the old ids. Plaintext is a page property, never a form field, audit row or notification.

surfaces.title: Estate onboarding wizard
surfaces.notes: Not applicable to this runtime (§36). The WordPress source is `WP_MCP_AI_Onboarding_Wizard` — a 2,414-line four-step first-run flow (welcome, provider key, assistant presets, finish) built around `wp_mcp_ai_activation_redirect`, a plugin-activation transient this runtime has no equivalent for. Its two real writes already have homes here: provider keys are `/ops/settings`, and seeding assistants from presets is `/admin/assistants`. Rebuilding the wizard would be a guided shell over surfaces that already exist, and duplicating the writes is how two settings paths start to disagree. `writer` corrected to `none`. If a first-run experience is ever wanted, the honest shape is a DERIVED checklist (is a provider key set, does an estate have an assistant) in the `site-health` / `assets` pattern — named as new work, not called onboarding parity.

surfaces.title: Site Health and connection pool
surfaces.projection: No reduction and no writer: every probe re-runs on page load and nothing is persisted, so a saved 'last checked' would be a lie the moment the page closes. Cross-estate by nature — the probes describe the runtime, not an estate. Configuration FLAGS only (is debug on, is the app key set, is the secure cookie on); no credential value is read or rendered. Eight probes port the eleven site_status_tests the WordPress plugin registers with core Site Health; file integrity, MCP schema compliance and per-model availability are not ported because they need WordPress itself. The status vocabulary is WordPress's on purpose: good, recommended, critical.
surfaces.notes: Shipped 2026-11-17 (§31). `writer` corrected from `ops` to `none`: a health page reads the runtime and writes nothing. The 'connection pool' half of the title is the queue probe (pending/failed depth); a pool inspector would need the queue driver's own metrics, which are not exposed here. Model availability and credentials validation are deliberately absent — the first is per-assistant data rather than a probe, and the second would require reading secrets to be meaningful.

surfaces.title: Identity and authentication
surfaces.projection: Renders on /admin/settings in the Authentication tab. Of the nineteen tenant-scope keys the plugin's seven sub-tabs define, eight are real (the Auth0 trio since §102, magic-link since §103, the three assistant REST gates since 159 slice 2 — plan §121), one renders inert, and ten are not rendered at all because they configure software this runtime does not have (plan §104). One key is still disabled at the FIELD level, not the surface level: `guest_token_lifetime` (this runtime has no anonymous chat to bound). It renders disabled, is refused by writableFor('admin'), and names its obstacle (UnimplementedSettings). The three REST gates left this list because they now have the split the old note said was missing: `EnsureAssistantRestEnabled` applies them to scoped machine principals only (§10, §5 rule 5). The ten absent-software keys are a different case and are hidden entirely (InapplicableSettings, plan §104): a disabled control still asserts the capability could be built here, and for a WordPress.com identity bridge or an SSE toggle on a route that is not served that is simply false. A key leaves either list the moment it gains a reader.
surfaces.notes: Corrected 2026-11-20 (Proposal 156). §36's 'nothing to port' was a false negative: it grepped identity_provider / IdentityProvider / saml / openid / oidc, and the WordPress surface is named auth0, so the search could not have found it. The surface exists in full — WP_MCP_AI_Auth0_Setup (admin.php?page=wp-mcp-ai-auth0-setup), JWKS plus iss/aud/scope verification in class-wp-mcp-ai-rest-authenticator.php, and the subject-to-user bridge in class-wp-mcp-ai-integration-auth0-github.php. The row was also mis-scoped: all nineteen keys are tenant scope because each is an estate's own trust configuration, so /ops is the wrong panel (§17 — it has no estate selected), hence audience tenant-admin, ops null, admin inert, writer admin. Six of the keys are API and tool policy rather than identity and are re-homed by D5; enable_simple_jwt_login and enable_wordpress_gravatar_bridge configure WordPress software this runtime does not have and are out of scope. The WordPress one-click wizard is deliberately not ported: its auto-configure handler derives auth0_domain from an unverified JWT payload (D6). I2 (plan §101) marked the unread keys inert; I3 (plan §102) made the Auth0 trio real — RS256 verification against the estate's JWKS with iss/aud/scope, mounted as `auth:sanctum,auth0`, with subjects linked by `nvoos:auth0-link` and denied when unlinked (D4, never matched by email); I4 (plan §103) made magic-link sign-in real — `/api/v1/magic-login/{request,confirm}`, hashed single-use tokens in `nvoos_magic_login_tokens`, 15-minute expiry, uniform answers, enabling estate resolved from the caller's memberships. Plan §104 then split the remaining surface: ten keys that configure absent software are hidden rather than disabled, and four stay inert. I5 then shipped (plan §110–§111, §116): OIDC just-in-time provisioning, deny-by-default, gated on `email_verified` AND a verified per-estate domain allowlist, provisioning `viewer` in the issuing estate and nothing else, with a pending-request surface and a daily digest. **I5 provisioned people and did not build a machine-principal model**, so these four keys are still inert — for the same obstacle, no longer waiting on a slice (§117). Note that `/api/v1/tools` DOES accept Auth0 tokens and is tenant-resolved: `routes/api.php` puts it inside `auth:sanctum,auth0` + `ResolveApiTenant`, so §102.4’s claim of its own `auth:sanctum` chain was wrong. What the catalogue listing lacks is a scope, not a guard, and tool EXECUTION has no route for any principal — the decision is Proposal 159. A first-party-versus-token-call split is now a decision of its own: nothing in this runtime distinguishes a browser principal from a token principal, and `guest_token_lifetime` still bounds a chat this runtime does not have. 2026-11-21 (§131): the surface state is `subset`, not `inert` — eight keys work and one FIELD is disabled. `inert` in the audit means a surface that renders and does nothing, which this one has not been since I3/I4/I5; the disabled key is `UnimplementedSettings`'s field-level state and stays explained rather than hidden.

surfaces.title: Access requests
surfaces.projection: Read and write, on one estate. Read: identities that authenticated and were not provisioned, with the gate that stopped them, and the estate's email-domain allowlist. Write: approve (creates the account and a viewer membership), dismiss, and add/verify/unverify/remove a domain. Every write calls AdminAuditLogger::recordResource(), because Livewire traffic is excluded from the request middleware (plan §25). Approving never grants a role other than viewer, and never attaches to an account that already holds the address (158 D4: users.email is unique, so attaching would be the takeover primitive 156 D4 forbids). Domain matching is exact after lowercasing and IDN normalisation, and an unverified domain provisions nobody (158 D3). A daily digest emails the estate's decision-makers the pending count, the addresses and the gate that stopped each one, with a link back here; it sends nothing when the list is empty (plan §111).
surfaces.notes: Proposal 149 §110, decisions 158 D2-D4. The surface exists because deny-by-default provisioning has a failure mode: the subject authenticates, gets a 403, and reads it as broken — which is what produces 'just turn it on for everyone'. Recording the refusal makes the dead end visible instead of silent. JIT itself is `enable_jit_provisioning` in the Authentication tab, default off; the digest is `enable_access_digest`, default on, because a reminder grants nothing. The digest is not a surface and so is not in `files` (that list is a strict set equality against app/Filament/, asserted by SurfaceOwnershipTest); it lives in app/Console/Commands/SendAccessDigest.php, app/Mail/AccessDigest.php and resources/views/emails/access-digest.blade.php, triggered by the `nvoos:access-digest` schedule entry.

surfaces.title: Asset inventory
surfaces.projection: No reduction and no writer: the register is DERIVED on every load from what the deployment actually contains — tables that exist with row counts, configured credentials as PRESENCE ONLY, registered providers, shipped packages and machine-read contracts. Nothing is stored, so there is nothing a second surface could disagree about, and an editable row would immediately stop describing reality. Cross-estate by nature: an information-asset register describes the deployment, not one estate's slice; the `owner` column carries the per-team split. Credential values are read transiently to reduce to a boolean and are never recorded, logged or rendered.
surfaces.notes: Shipped 2026-11-17 (§33). §32's assumption was wrong and is corrected here: the WordPress source (`WP_MCP_AI_Asset_Inventory`) is auto-discovered, not a hand-maintained CRUD register — it walks code directories, probes option presence, lists integrations, counts CPTs and stores the result in an option refreshed weekly. It persists only because its discovery walks the plugin tree; this runtime's discovery is a handful of cheap queries, so a stored snapshot would go stale on the next migration. `writer` corrected from `ops` to `none`. Classification vocabulary and the eight asset types are copied verbatim from the WordPress constants so `reports` can key off the same labels.

surfaces.title: Dataset browser
surfaces.projection: Reference catalogue, identical for every estate and not reduced anywhere: it lists the ten HuggingFace dataset tools the registry serves, the endpoint each one calls (read from the tool's own constant), and the curated datasets the recommended-datasets tool answers from. The only estate-specific fact on the page is where a token is configured, and the page names that location rather than reading the secret.
surfaces.notes: Researched three times, 2026-11-17, and the conclusion moved twice before it settled (§35). (1) §32 said 'blocked on an HF client, a quota'd store and a registry'. (2) The classes DO exist — lib/core ships eleven HuggingFace dataset tools including huggingface_dataset_preview_rows and huggingface_recommended_datasets — so a browser looked free. (3) Verified in the registry: none of them was registered. They were listed in lib/core/resources/tool-readiness.php as `unverified` ('Auto-added by the auditor; not classified yet') and ManifestToolRegistrar serves only servable tools, so a browser would have advertised datasets this runtime could not use — the §32 objection, evidenced rather than assumed. UNBLOCK = classify those eleven tools or mark them deliberately unavailable. 2026-11-19 (§85): all eleven became `unavailable` with the datasets-server and token requirement recorded. 2026-11-19 (§91): per-tool evidence against a recording client, ten flipped to `ready` and one (recommended_datasets) to `pure`, and `parity: port` declared. 2026-11-19 (§95): the browser shipped — READ-ONLY, deriving its endpoints from each tool's `ENDPOINT` constant and its starting points from `HuggingFaceRecommendedDatasetsTool::datasets()`, so no second declaration exists to drift. It deliberately has no 'run' action: argument validation and provider errors belong to chat and to POST /api/v1/tools, not to a page whose job is to describe the catalogue. `writer` stays `none`: browsing never writes.

surfaces.title: Conversation import
surfaces.projection: A deliberately narrow first version (Â§37). Accepted: pasted JSON in two shapes â€” ShareGPT (`[{conversations: [{from, value}]}]`) and generic (`[{session_id, messages: [{role, content}]}]`). Caps enforced on the string before storage: 2,097,152 bytes, 500 conversations, 200 messages per conversation (excess truncated and reported). The target estate is chosen on the page (selector, default `default`); the import pins `TenantContext` for the action only and an unknown estate refuses before any write. NOT ported from WordPress: zip archives (an archive reader needs entry-name validation and a decompression limit), JSONL streaming (needs a temp file, which a paste avoids), the Claude / Gemini / OpenAI-JSONL adapters, media handling, the memory miner, the privacy filter, and the async queue (import is synchronous and bounded instead). Import is idempotent because TranscriptStoreInterface::save() upserts by session_id and the key is derived deterministically; imported text is scrubbed to valid UTF-8 and roles come from a closed set.
surfaces.notes: Shipped as `subset` 2026-11-17 (Â§37). Â§32 called this 'a feature rather than a page ... needs its own proposal'; that was right about the WordPress subsystem (fifteen classes) and wrong about the smallest useful slice â€” two shapes, synchronous, capped, upsert-by-session is a genuine import. Paste rather than upload on purpose: an upload path needs a temporary file store, a MIME gate and a size check before the bytes are readable, and this runtime has not configured one for imports. `writer: ops` is correct and this is one of the few rows where a state of `subset` still writes. The Â§37.5 estate-selector gap closed 2026-11-18: the page names its target, pins `TenantContext` for the action and restores it, refuses an unknown estate before any write, and records the estate on the audit row.

surfaces.title: Compliance reports
surfaces.projection: Cross-estate and unreduced: a compliance report evidences the whole deployment, not one estate. Two sections only — assets (derived by AssetRegister) and audit trail (AuditTrail over nvoos_admin_audit). WordPress also emits controls, risks, evidence and frameworks from a Pro compliance database this runtime does not have; those are OMITTED rather than emitted empty, because a 'Risks' heading with no rows reads as 'no risks', which is a claim rather than an absence. Formats are CSV and JSON: the WordPress generator also returns an error for PDF/DOCX/Excel, and a report generator that pulls in a PDF engine to render one table is the wrong trade. No standalone HTML artifact — this page is the HTML report.
surfaces.notes: Shipped 2026-11-17 (§34). `writer` stays `ops`, and that is the distinction worth keeping: the state is `read-only` because the surface writes no report data — every file is streamed from memory and nothing is persisted — but each download records an audit row, so the layer does own one write. The audit row records format and counts, never content. The page and both downloads serialise one ComplianceReport, so there is no second renderer to drift.

surfaces.title: Chat profiles (read-only enforcement)
surfaces.notes: Enforcement shipped (Proposal 149 §174). This runtime now has all three pieces the old note said were missing: a two-profile registry in nvoos/core (`write`/`read-only`), a per-user preference on `users.chat_profile`, and a monotonic `ChatProfileGuard` that delegates the flag decision to `ReadOnlyToolGuard`, registered in the tool registry. `GET`/`PUT /api/v1/chat-profile` is the writer, which is why `writer` moved from `none` to `console`: the API is the console's write path. `console` stays null because the SPA has no `console-endpoints.json` key for it yet. The admin page is still `absent`, now for a product reason rather than a missing prerequisite — the profile is a per-user preference, so a tenant-admin page that set someone else's would be an authority grant, not a preference. Still unported and recorded: the guest profile (there is no anonymous chat surface here; `guest_token_lifetime` is inert for that reason), the advisory system-prompt hint, and the Pro profile-registration filter.

surfaces.title: Admin audit log
surfaces.projection: Cross-estate on purpose, and that is not a reduction to bypass: an operator asking what happened on one estate needs that estate's rows plus the operator actions that touched it, and the latter carry no estate at all. Both row kinds are shown — request rows (resource null, 'who tried and was refused') and record rows (resource set, 'what changed') — because showing only the second hides every 403/422. Payload and diff columns are redacted at write time by AdminAuditLogger::redact(); this reader does not re-redact, since the write-time pass runs on every path and a second pass would give false confidence.
surfaces.notes: Read-only view of nvoos_admin_audit. Append-only by construction; no surface may write it. Shipped 2026-11-17 (§25) with App\Models\AdminAudit and App\Support\Admin\AuditTrail. The same slice made the estate credential revoke write a record row: panel actions travel over Livewire's /livewire/update, which AuditAdminRequests deliberately skips, so a destructive panel action would otherwise leave no trace at all.

surfaces.title: Machine-executable tools
surfaces.projection: Operator-scope and unreduced: it writes the platform setting the machine-principal tool gate reads, so there is no estate projection to reduce. Only tools the readiness manifest calls servable are listed, and a row that came from `config/oos.machine_tools` has no remove action — the page may widen what a deploy allowed, never narrow it. Annotations are shown as a veto ('If a machine ran it'), not as a guarantee.
surfaces.notes: No WordPress equivalent: the WP admin has no machine-principal surface, so this is a Laravel-only operator surface recorded rather than left implicit. Shipped 2026-11-21 (149 §128).

surfaces.title: Machine credentials
surfaces.projection: Machine tokens only, identified by the `oos-machine:` prefix; a token whose name is personal or assistant-scoped is not listed and cannot be revoked through this page. Owner and scopes are shown because a machine credential carries an assistant's authority rather than a person's — the operator who issued it is the operator who revokes it.
surfaces.notes: No WordPress equivalent: the WP admin has no machine-principal credentials. The inventory's read-only rule for a person's own tokens is unchanged and deliberate. Shipped 2026-11-21 (149 §129).
